## Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Explain how Java runs on all platforms.
- Install and switch between Java versions with SDKMAN!.
- Develop Java applications with IntelliJ IDEA and Maven.
- Manage dependencies and build a distributable JAR with Maven.
- Write and run a first unit test.

::: {.callout-important}
The tools (SDKMAN!, Java 25, Maven, IntelliJ IDEA) were installed in
[chapter 00](00-environment-setup.qmd). If any verification of its final
checklist fails, fix that first.
:::

## Java

> Java is a general-purpose, class-based, object-oriented programming
> language. It is intended to let programmers write once, run anywhere
> (WORA). (<https://www.java.com/>)

Created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now Oracle) and released in
1995, Java remains one of the most used languages, especially for
client-server applications.

### The Java virtual machine

Java source code is compiled to **bytecode**, which is executed by the
**Java virtual machine (JVM)**. The same compiled code runs on every
platform that has a JVM: that is what makes Java portable.

Many JVM implementations exist. Two packages matter to you:

- The **JDK** (Java Development Kit): what you need to *develop*.
- The **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment): what you need to *run*.

We use the **Eclipse Temurin** distribution.

### Versions and version managers

Java evolves in versions, with a **Long Term Support (LTS)** release
every two years. **Java 25** is the current LTS and the version of this
course.

Projects can require different Java versions, so developers use a version
manager. You installed [SDKMAN!](https://sdkman.io/) in chapter 00: it
installs and switches between versions cleanly. Within a project, use the
same version as the other developers.

### Compiling and running Java programs

Given a `HelloWorld.java` file:

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String message = "Hello, world!";

        System.out.println(message);
    }
}
```

Compile it with `javac` and run the bytecode with `java`:

```sh
javac HelloWorld.java
java HelloWorld
```

Real applications are packaged into a **JAR** (Java ARchive) file: a ZIP
containing the bytecode and resources, runnable anywhere Java is
installed:

```sh
java -Xmx1024M -Xms1024M -jar minecraft_server.1.21.jar nogui
```

(Yes, the Minecraft server is a JAR. `-Xmx` and `-Xms` set the maximum
and initial memory of the JVM, one of many tuning knobs.)

### Garbage collection

Java manages memory automatically: no manual allocation and freeing as in
C or C++. The **garbage collector** (GC) runs periodically and frees
objects that are no longer referenced (out of scope or set to `null`).

## IntelliJ IDEA

> IntelliJ IDEA is an integrated development environment (IDE) written in
> Java for developing computer software.
> (<https://www.jetbrains.com/idea/>)

IntelliJ IDEA is the reference IDE for Java development. It exists in two
editions: **Community** (free, sufficient for this course) and
**Ultimate** (paid, free for you with the
[student license](https://www.jetbrains.com/community/education/#students)).
Another IDE is allowed, but IntelliJ is what we support.

### Configuration files and Git

When you create a project, IntelliJ creates a `.idea` directory:

- Some files hold **project configuration**, shared by all developers.
  They are committed, so everyone gets the same setup.
- Some files hold **local configuration**, specific to your machine.
  They must be ignored by Git.

You will clean this up in the exercises.

## Maven

> Apache Maven is a software project management and comprehension tool.
> (<https://maven.apache.org/>)

Maven is two things at once:

- A **dependency manager**: it downloads and manages the external
  libraries your application uses.
- A **build automation tool**: it compiles, tests and packages your
  application, the same way on every machine.

### Project structure

Maven defines a standard directory layout, so every developer finds
everything in the same place:

```text
my-project/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/          # application sources
    │   └── resources/     # config files, assets
    └── test/
        └── java/          # unit tests
```

### The `pom.xml` file

The Project Object Model (POM) file is the core of a Maven project,
shared by all developers. Its main sections:

- `groupId`: the namespace of the project (the organization).
- `artifactId`: the name of the project.
- `version`: the version of the project.
- `dependencies`: the external libraries used by the application.
- `build`/`plugins`: how the application is compiled, tested, packaged.

The `artifactId` and `version` determine the name of the generated JAR.

::: {.callout-note}
**Plugin or dependency?** A *plugin* performs a build task (compile,
package) and does not end up in your JAR. A *dependency* is a library
your code uses, and it ships with your application.
:::

### The Maven lifecycle

Maven organizes the build around three standard **lifecycles**:

- **default**: builds the project (compile, test, package, deploy).
- **clean**: deletes the build outputs (`target/`).
- **site**: generates documentation and reports (not used in this
  course).

Each lifecycle is a **sequence of phases**, the logical steps of the
build. The main phases of the default lifecycle, in order:

| Phase | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| `validate` | check the project is correct and complete |
| `compile` | compile the source code |
| `test` | run the unit tests |
| `package` | package the compiled code into a JAR |
| `verify` | run checks on integration test results |
| `install` | install the JAR into your local repository |
| `deploy` | copy the JAR to a remote repository |

The rule that explains most Maven behavior: **running a phase runs all
the previous phases of its lifecycle**. `./mvnw package` actually runs
`validate`, `compile`, `test`, then `package`. And `./mvnw clean package`
combines two lifecycles: clean up, then build.

A **goal** is a single task provided by a plugin. Goals are **bound to
phases**: when a phase runs, its goals run. Default bindings include:

- `compile` phase: runs the `compiler:compile` goal.
- `test` phase: runs the `surefire:test` goal.
- `package` phase: runs the `jar:jar` goal.

A goal can also run directly, outside any lifecycle: you already did it
with `mvn wrapper:wrapper`, and `./mvnw dependency:tree` (try it later)
prints your dependency tree without building anything.

In short: a **lifecycle** is the overall process, a **phase** is a step
in it, a **goal** is the plugin action executed at that step, and the
task is the actual work done (turning `.java` files into `.class`
files).

### Maven Central

The [Maven Repository](https://mvnrepository.com/) indexes the public
libraries you can use. Search a library, copy its dependency declaration
into your `pom.xml`, and Maven downloads it automatically, transitive
dependencies included.

### The Maven wrapper

The **Maven wrapper** is a small script (`mvnw` on Linux/macOS,
`mvnw.cmd` on Windows) committed to the repository. It downloads and runs
a pinned version of Maven, so every developer (and every server) builds
with the same version, without installing Maven first. Once initialized,
use `./mvnw` instead of `mvn`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Maven cheat sheet"}
```sh
./mvnw dependency:go-offline   # download all dependencies
./mvnw clean                   # delete compiled classes
./mvnw compile                 # compile the source code
./mvnw test                    # run the unit tests
./mvnw package                 # package the application
./mvnw clean package           # several phases in one command
```
:::

## Unit tests

A **unit test** is code that verifies a small piece of your code: given
this input, this function must return that output. Tests live in
`src/test/java`, mirror your package structure, and run in the `test`
phase, so **a broken test fails the build** before a broken JAR reaches
anyone.

The standard library is [JUnit](https://junit.org/). A test is a method
annotated with `@Test` that makes assertions:

```java
package ch.heigvd;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class GreetingTest {

  @Test
  void greetsByName() {
    assertEquals("Hello DAI!", Greeting.greet("DAI"));
  }
}
```

You will write your first test in the exercises, and tests will be
expected in your practical works.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Juggle Java versions {#sec-ex1}

Projects will not always use the version you have. Practice switching
with SDKMAN!:

```sh
# List what is available and installed
sdk list java

# Install the PREVIOUS LTS (21) next to your Java 25
sdk install java <21-version>-tem

# Use it in the current terminal only
sdk use java <21-version>-tem
java --version

# Back to Java 25 as the default everywhere
sdk default java <25-version>-tem
java --version
```

**Verification**: `java --version` shows 21 after `sdk use`, and 25 again
in a new terminal.

### Exercise 2: Create the Maven project {#sec-ex2}

1. In IntelliJ IDEA, create a **New Project** with the **Maven** build
   system. Set the group ID to `ch.heigvd`, the artifact ID to
   `java-intellij-idea-and-maven`, and **check that the selected JDK is
   the latest LTS (25)**.
2. Open the `Main` file and press **Play**: the Run tab prints
   `Hello World!`.
3. In the IntelliJ terminal, initialize the **Maven wrapper**:

```sh
mvn wrapper:wrapper
```

This creates `mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd` and `.mvn/wrapper/`, all committed to
Git. From now on, use `./mvnw`.

**Verification**: `./mvnw --version` prints Maven, running on Java 25.

::: {.callout-tip}
Store the build as an IntelliJ **Run/Debug configuration** (type Maven,
command `dependency:go-offline clean compile package`, check *Store as
project file*): you and the graders can then build with one click.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Windows + WSL: IntelliJ and the Maven wrapper"}
Recent IntelliJ versions have a bug selecting *Use Maven wrapper* in a
Run/Debug configuration on WSL. If it fails, set it at the IDE level
instead: **Settings > Build, Execution, Deployment > Build Tools >
Maven**, set *Maven home path* to *Use Maven wrapper*, and keep *Inherit
from settings* checked in the configuration. Related reports:
[IDEA-370490](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IDEA-370490),
[IDEA-368924](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IDEA-368924).
:::

### Exercise 3: Package a JAR {#sec-ex3}

Tell Maven what the entry point of your JAR is, by adding the
`maven-jar-plugin` to the `<build><plugins>` section of your `pom.xml`
(check the
[latest version](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.apache.maven.plugins/maven-jar-plugin)):

```xml
<plugin>
  <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.2</version>
  <configuration>
    <archive>
      <manifest>
        <mainClass>ch.heigvd.Main</mainClass>
      </manifest>
    </archive>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
```

::: {.callout-important}
Do not blindly copy-paste snippets, here or anywhere. Read them and adapt
them to your project.
:::

Then build and run:

```sh
./mvnw dependency:go-offline
./mvnw package
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

**Verification**: the application output appears, this time from a JAR
you could hand to anyone with Java installed.

### Exercise 4: A real CLI with picocli {#sec-ex4}

> Picocli aims to be the easiest way to create rich command line
> applications that can run on and off the JVM. (<https://picocli.info/>)

Your first external dependency. Add picocli to the `<dependencies>`
section (check the
[latest version](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/info.picocli/picocli)):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>info.picocli</groupId>
  <artifactId>picocli</artifactId>
  <version>4.7.7</version>
</dependency>
```

Replace `src/main/java/ch/heigvd/Main.java` with a first picocli command:

```java
package ch.heigvd;

import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import picocli.CommandLine;

@CommandLine.Command(
    name = "hello",
    description = "Print a 'Hello World!' type of message.",
    version = "1.0.0",
    showDefaultValues = true,
    mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
class Main implements Callable<Integer> {

  @CommandLine.Parameters(
      index = "0",
      description = "The name of the user.",
      defaultValue = "World")
  protected String name;

  @Override
  public Integer call() {
    System.out.println("Hello " + name + "!");
    return 0;
  }

  public static void main(String... args) {
    int exitCode = new CommandLine(new Main()).execute(args);

    System.exit(exitCode);
  }
}
```

`@CommandLine.Command` defines a command, `@CommandLine.Parameters` a
positional argument, and `call()` runs when the command executes.

::: {.callout-tip}
IntelliJ does not recognize `CommandLine`? Right-click the project >
**Maven** > **Reload project**.
:::

Package the JAR again and run it. **It fails**:

```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: picocli/CommandLine
```

This error is worth understanding: `maven-jar-plugin` does **not**
include dependencies in the JAR. Your code is there, picocli is not.
(See [Go further](#go-further) for what the plugin *can* do about
dependencies, and why it is not enough.)
Replace the `maven-jar-plugin` block with the `maven-shade-plugin`, which
builds a JAR with all dependencies included (check the
[latest version](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.apache.maven.plugins/maven-shade-plugin)):

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.6.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals>
        <goal>shade</goal>
      </goals>
      <phase>package</phase>
      <configuration>
        <transformers>
          <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer">
            <mainClass>ch.heigvd.Main</mainClass>
          </transformer>
          <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.DontIncludeResourceTransformer">
            <resource>MANIFEST.MF</resource>
          </transformer>
        </transformers>
      </configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

Rebuild and run. `target/` now also contains an `original-...jar` (the
one without dependencies) and a `dependency-reduced-pom.xml`, both
by-products of shading.

**Verification**:

```sh
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar --help
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar "DAI student"
```

The help message and `Hello DAI student!` appear.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is packaging so complicated?"}
Java builds many kinds of artifacts (libraries, web applications, desktop
applications), each with different packaging needs, so Maven does not
assume dependencies belong inside the JAR. For a standalone CLI they do,
hence the shade plugin. Deeper build topics come in later teaching units.
:::

### Exercise 5: Subcommands {#sec-ex5}

Real CLIs have subcommands (think `git commit`, `git push`). Refactor
into a `hello` and a `goodbye` subcommand. Create
`src/main/java/ch/heigvd/commands/Hello.java`:

```java
package ch.heigvd.commands;

import ch.heigvd.Main;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import picocli.CommandLine;

@CommandLine.Command(name = "hello", description = "Print a 'Hello World!' type of message.")
public class Hello implements Callable<Integer> {

  @CommandLine.ParentCommand protected Main parent;

  @CommandLine.Option(
      names = {"-g", "--greetings"},
      description = "The greetings to address the user.",
      defaultValue = "Hello")
  protected String greetings;

  @Override
  public Integer call() {
    System.out.println(greetings + " " + parent.getName() + "!");
    return 0;
  }
}
```

Create `Goodbye.java` in the same package on the same model (option
`-f`/`--farewells`, default `Goodbye`). Then update `Main.java`:

```java
package ch.heigvd;

import ch.heigvd.commands.Goodbye;
import ch.heigvd.commands.Hello;
import java.io.File;
import picocli.CommandLine;

@CommandLine.Command(
    description = "A small CLI with subcommands to demonstrate picocli.",
    version = "1.0.0",
    showDefaultValues = true,
    subcommands = {
      Hello.class,
      Goodbye.class,
    },
    scope = CommandLine.ScopeType.INHERIT,
    mixinStandardHelpOptions = true)
public class Main {

  @CommandLine.Parameters(
      index = "0",
      description = "The name of the user.",
      defaultValue = "World")
  protected String name;

  public String getName() {
    return this.name;
  }

  public static void main(String[] args) {
    String jarFilename =
        new File(Main.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().getPath())
            .getName();

    int exitCode = new CommandLine(new Main()).setCommandName(jarFilename).execute(args);

    System.exit(exitCode);
  }
}
```

New pieces: `subcommands` registers them, `scope = INHERIT` shares the
parent's options, `@CommandLine.ParentCommand` gives a subcommand access
to its parent, and `@CommandLine.Option` defines a `-x`/`--xyz` style
argument.

**Verification**:

```sh
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar hello
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \
  "étudiant.e de DAI" hello --greetings "Bonjour"
java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar \
  "étudiant.e de DAI" goodbye --farewells "Au revoir"
```

picocli will be used in most practical works. Its
[documentation](https://picocli.info/) is excellent, explore it.

### Exercise 6: A first unit test {#sec-ex6}

1. Add JUnit to your `<dependencies>` (check the
   [latest version](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.junit.jupiter/junit-jupiter),
   scope `test` so it does not ship in your JAR):

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
  <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
  <version>5.13.4</version>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

2. Extract the greeting logic into a testable method (e.g. a
   `Greeting.greet(String greetings, String name)` static method that
   your commands call), and write a test for it in
   `src/test/java/ch/heigvd/GreetingTest.java` (model in the
   [Unit tests](#unit-tests) section).
3. Run the tests:

```sh
./mvnw test
```

**Verification**: the build reports your test passing. Break the expected
string on purpose, run again, and watch the build fail. That is the
point.

### Exercise 7: Publish on GitHub {#sec-ex7}

Everything you learned in [chapter 02](02-git-github.qmd), applied:

1. `git init --initial-branch=main` in the project.
2. **Clean the `.gitignore`**: IntelliJ generates one full of rules for
   tools you do not use. Only ignore what your project actually
   produces:

```gitignore
## IntelliJ IDEA
.idea/libraries/
.idea/shelf/
.idea/compiler.xml
.idea/jarRepositories.xml
.idea/modules.xml
.idea/workspace.xml
*.iws
*.iml
*.ipr

## Linux
*~

## macOS
.DS_Store

## Maven
target/

## Windows
Thumbs.db
[Dd]esktop.ini
```

   Delete the `.idea/.gitignore` file.

3. Write a `README.md`: what the project is, how to build it, how to run
   it. It is the first thing anyone (including the graders) reads.
4. Create an **empty** GitHub repository (no README, license or
   gitignore), then:

```sh
git remote add origin <your repository ssh url>
git add .
git status    # check that target/ and local .idea files are NOT staged
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push --set-upstream origin main
```

5. Share the repository link in the
   [GitHub Discussions]({{< var discussions-url >}}) (category *Show and
   tell*).

**Verification**: the repository on GitHub shows your code, your README,
your signed commits, and no `target/` directory.

## Test your knowledge

- How can Java run on all platforms?
- How do you install and switch between Java versions?
- Why must some files created by IntelliJ IDEA be ignored by Git?
- What is the purpose of the `pom.xml` file?
- What is the difference between a Maven plugin and a dependency?
- Why did the JAR fail to run before the shade plugin, and what changed?
- What happens to the build when a unit test fails, and why is that
  useful?

## Go further

Optional content: useful general knowledge, not required for the
evaluations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why maven-jar-plugin cannot ship your dependencies"}
`maven-jar-plugin` has a partial answer to the dependency problem:

```xml
<manifest>
  <addClasspath>true</addClasspath>
  <mainClass>ch.heigvd.Main</mainClass>
</manifest>
```

`addClasspath` writes a line like `Class-Path: picocli-4.7.7.jar` into
the JAR's `MANIFEST.MF`. At run time, Java then looks for those JARs
**next to yours on disk**. Your JAR still does not *contain* picocli, it
only points at it, so you would have to distribute the dependency JARs
alongside your application. That is why a standalone CLI uses the shade
plugin instead: one self-contained JAR, nothing else to ship.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Spotless: automatic code formatting"}
[Spotless](https://github.com/diffplug/spotless/tree/main/plugin-maven)
formats your Java files and `pom.xml` automatically (Google Java Format),
and fails the build when the formatting is off. Add the
`spotless-maven-plugin` to your build plugins with the `check` goal bound
to the `package` phase, then:

```sh
./mvnw spotless:check   # report formatting issues
./mvnw spotless:apply   # fix them
```

Consistent formatting is a gift to your team (and to the graders).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Alternatives"}
JVM languages: [Kotlin](https://kotlinlang.org/),
[Scala](https://www.scala-lang.org/), [Groovy](https://groovy-lang.org/).
Build tools: [Gradle](https://gradle.org/), [Ant](https://ant.apache.org/),
[Bazel](https://bazel.build/). Version manager:
[asdf](https://asdf-vm.com/). CLI libraries elsewhere:
[clap](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap) (Rust),
[Cobra](https://github.com/spf13/cobra) (Go).
:::
